articles.title: If AI cannot be trusted in a classroom, why should it be trusted in orbit?
articles.author: Qurat-Ul-Ain Shabbir

paras.en: On September 9, 2026, Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s alignment science lead, said on social media that he personally believed there was a greater than 10% chance that artificial intelligence could kill all of humanity within the next decade. He was responding to Jacob Coxon, a researcher who had just resigned from Anthropic after working on pretraining at both that company and OpenAI, and who wrote in his own resignation thread that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Hubinger did not walk the claim back. He confirmed it, while noting that the danger he had in mind was not today’s models but a future superintelligence for which the industry does not yet have a solved alignment plan.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Coming from the safety lead at one of the two or three companies most responsible for the technology’s current trajectory, this was not a fringe warning. It was, in effect, an admission from inside the room.

The exchange was framed almost entirely around AI in the abstract: chatbots, agents, the eventual arrival of self-improving systems. But the domain where this risk is least abstract and most immediate is not a hypothetical future superintelligence. It is the set of systems already being integrated into nuclear early warning satellites, missile-tracking constellations and the command and control architecture that decides, in minutes, whether a detected launch is real. If a company’s own safety researchers are willing to say on the record that current AI development carries a double-digit chance of civilizational catastrophe, the question that follows is not academic: What happens when systems built by that same industry, with that same acknowledged uncertainty, are the ones watching for nuclear launches from orbit and feeding what they see directly into the decision loop of nuclear-armed states?
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The nuclear-space nexus is where AI safety debate stops being abstract
This is the nuclear space nexus, and it is where the abstract AI safety debate stops being abstract.

The mechanism runs through space architecture itself. Satellite constellations, orbital processing units and ground relay stations are the physical layer that decides what a nuclear armed state believes is happening in the world. The AI systems currently doing that work are narrow, frozen weight models, convolutional networks for image classification, sensor fusion algorithms for combining radar and satellite feeds, nothing resembling the self improving superintelligence Coxon and Hubinger were warning about. That distinction is precisely what makes the space layer worth examining rather than dismissing.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: For decades, that layer worked on a simple “bent pipe” model: satellites captured raw infrared and radar data and beamed it down to Earth for human analysts to interpret. That model is being replaced. Modern space architecture is shifting toward onboard edge AI, with computer vision models embedded directly into satellite payloads deciding, in orbit, what counts as a missile plume before a human ever sees the raw image. At the same time, the shift from a handful of large geostationary satellites to proliferated low Earth orbit constellations of thousands of smaller satellites means no human team can parse the feeds directly. Data fusion platforms now do that work, aggregating radar, imagery and signals intelligence into a single real time track. Even a narrow, well tested model compresses the time available for human judgment, since the entire argument for automating this layer is that orbital and hypersonic threats move faster than people can react to.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And while today’s systems are not the unaligned frontier models Coxon feared, they still introduce a structural risk: the same edge processing and data fusion architecture being built now is the substrate that a future self improving system, if one ever gained access to military networks, would inherit and exploit. A false positive in this setting is not a chatbot hallucination. It is a satellite misreading a solar flare or a glint of debris as a missile plume, and passing that reading up a chain of command that may have only minutes to decide whether to believe it.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: A useful, if unlikely, point of comparison arrived days apart from the Hubinger exchange. On September 2, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced a one-year moratorium on generative AI for public school students through eighth grade, affecting nearly 600,000 children and disabling AI functions in dozens of previously approved classroom programs. The justification was not that the technology does not work. It was that the city could not yet be confident it belonged in a setting where the cost of getting it wrong, a child’s developing capacity to think for herself, was too important to risk on a technology still being evaluated.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “Children need teachers and human connection in order to learn and in order to grow,” Mamdani said. “We hold an obligation to do the same” when it comes to AI’s role in that development.

It is worth sitting with the asymmetry this produces. New York City possesses centralized, enforceable authority over what software runs on its own school-issued devices, and used that authority to pause AI in a setting where the downside of error is developmental, not existential. Nuclear-armed states, by contrast, are integrating comparable AI systems into early warning and command infrastructure where the downside of error is civilizational, and there is no equivalent central authority capable of imposing a comparable pause. If the mere possibility of AI eroding a child’s critical thinking was sufficient grounds for New York City to disable the technology outright pending further study, the far larger and more immediate possibility of AI misreading a satellite feed and compressing a nuclear decision to seconds deserves at least the same precautionary instinct, applied to the domain where a mistake cannot be undone.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The honest complication is that a school district and the international nuclear order are not remotely comparable in their capacity to act on that instinct. A ban is enforceable when one authority controls the devices in question; it is close to unenforceable when the object being restricted is software that can be updated remotely over an encrypted satellite uplink, and when no state trusts another enough to grant the kind of intrusive access that verifying compliance would require. This is precisely the gap that existing international efforts are now trying, with limited success, to close.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: International bodies efforts to establish global norms regarding AI and nuclear command

The most direct attempt sits at the United Nations. On December 1, 2025, the General Assembly adopted Resolution A/RES/80/23 on the risks of integrating artificial intelligence into nuclear command, control, and communications, passing 118 to 9 with 44 abstentions. The resolution calls on states to adopt and publish national policies affirming that AI-enabled NC3 systems will remain under human control and will not be capable of autonomously initiating a nuclear launch decision. That it passed with broad support is meaningful. That nine states voted against it, and that France, a nuclear power that itself insists human control must be preserved at every critical stage of a launch decision, was reportedly among them, says something sharper about how far declaratory consensus is from binding practice.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Alongside the UN process, the Summit on Responsible AI in the Military Domain, known as REAIM, has become the closest thing to a running multilateral forum on this question. Its third summit was held in A Coruña, Spain, on February 4 and 5, following earlier summits in The Hague in 2023 and Seoul in 2024. It was explicitly framed as an attempt to move from declared principles to “concrete, practical and realistic steps.” That framing was itself a quiet admission that the first two summits had not managed the transition. The 2026 outcome document was endorsed by only 39 states, down from more than 60 in 2024, a decline several analysts have linked to deteriorating relations among the major AI and nuclear powers rather than to any narrowing of the underlying risk.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: What both processes share is the same structural weakness: They are norm-setting exercises operating in a domain where the thing being regulated, software, cannot be counted, inspected or verified the way a missile silo can. A state can comply with the letter of a resolution on human control while still deploying an AI system that filters, prioritizes and frames the sensor data a human ultimately sees, shaping the decision long before a human formally makes it. The requirement that a person retain final authority does very little if that person’s picture of reality has already been constructed by a model no outside party can audit.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: How independent research bodies evaluate these UN blueprints

Independent research bodies evaluating these blueprints have converged on a similar diagnosis. In an assessment of the UNGA resolution published shortly after its adoption, the Observer Research Foundation concluded that the measure signals a genuine and broadly shared anxiety among states, but that it remains constrained by exactly the fault lines one would expect: the divide between nuclear and non-nuclear states, the reluctance of major nuclear powers to accept binding restrictions on capabilities they consider central to deterrence and the fact that the resolution’s core language, human control and oversight, was never defined with enough technical precision to be verified rather than merely declared. The same critique applies to REAIM’s outcome documents, which rely on states to describe their own compliance rather than submitting to any external check. Both processes are, in the assessment of the researchers who study them, aspirational rather than enforceable, useful for establishing that a problem is taken seriously, but not yet capable of constraining the behavior of the states whose behavior actually matters.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: This is, in effect, the diplomatic community’s answer to the technical impossibility of a blanket prohibition. Recognizing this, the UN General Assembly and allied processes have instead pursued a narrower, more realistic strategy: isolating AI from specific, high-consequence use cases, nuclear launch authority chief among them, rather than attempting to regulate military AI as a single undifferentiated category. Resolution A/RES/80/23 is itself an example of this approach in practice. It does not ban AI from space or defence systems generally; it targets one function, the initiation of a nuclear launch decision and insists that function alone remain exclusively human. The strategy is sound in principle. Its weakness, as the evaluations above make clear, is that use-case segregation only works if the boundary between an isolated function and the surrounding system can actually be verified.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: None of this means the underlying comparison to Mamdani’s classroom ban should be read too literally. What it usefully exposes is the gap between the precautionary standard a single city was willing to apply to a developmental risk and the precautionary standard the international system has so far been able to apply to an existential one. The nuclear order, by contrast, continues to integrate AI into its most sensitive systems while the very researchers building the underlying technology are, in public, on the record, unable to rule out a double-digit chance of civilizational catastrophe. The core policy question this raises is not whether AI can be kept out of nuclear command systems entirely.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: It is whether the international community can move from resolutions that describe the danger, and use-case boundaries that sound precise on paper, to verification mechanisms that actually constrain it, before the gap between declared principle and deployed practice is tested by a false alarm instead of a vote count.

articles.title: NaviGate successfully demonstrates onboard precise orbit determination aboard D-Orbit’s ION Satellite Carrier
articles.author: NaviGate

paras.en: ROME, 30/09/2026 – NaviGate, an Italian space technology company spun out of Sapienza University of Rome, has successfully completed the in-orbit demonstration (IoD) of NaviCode Caravel, its autonomous onboard precise orbit determination software, aboard an ION Satellite Carrier operated by D-Orbit. During the demonstration, NaviCode Caravel ran directly on the satellite’s onboard computer, computing the spacecraft’s position in real time using only the raw data of the GNSS receiver already onboard, with no additional hardware.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Today, knowing precisely where a satellite is remains largely a ground-based activity: operators rely on dedicated infrastructure, specialized flight dynamics teams, and repeated ground contacts to accurately reconstruct and predict the orbit of each spacecraft. As constellations grow in size and missions become more responsive, this approach turns into a bottleneck in terms of cost, workload, and reaction time. NaviCode Caravel moves precise orbit determination onboard: a software-only product that transforms the raw measurements of the GNSS receiver a satellite already carries into high-accuracy, real-time knowledge of its own position, available directly where operational decisions are made. Beyond determining where the satellite is now, Caravel can also predict where it will be, together with a measure of how reliable that prediction is, giving the spacecraft the forward-looking awareness it needs to anticipate upcoming events, such as ground station contacts or payload operations, and manage them autonomously onboard.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The demonstration was carried out through D-Orbit’s Software In-Orbit Demonstration service and structured in two phases. NaviCode Caravel was first validated on the ground on an engineering model replicating the in-orbit computing environment. The application was then uploaded to an ION Satellite Carrier already in orbit and executed onboard, processing real flight telemetry from the spacecraft’s GNSS receiver across multiple runs.

The software executed nominally onboard and in real time without anomalies. Onboard positioning reached a best-case formal uncertainty of 5.2 cm, with mean values in the decimeter range across the runs, using GPS-only measurements. NaviGate then verified the onboard solutions on the ground, proving them consistent with the reference orbits reconstructed through classical ground-based precise orbit determination performed with GODOT, the European Space Agency’s flight dynamics software. NaviCode Caravel is also designed to process multi-constellation GNSS data and correction services such as SBAS and Galileo HAS, enabling even higher accuracy in operational deployments.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “Satellites still depend heavily on the ground to know exactly where they are and where they will be. NaviCode Caravel changes that: it is a software product that lets a satellite compute its own position with high accuracy, in real time, using the GNSS receiver it already carries, with no new hardware,” said Andrea Sesta, Chief Technology Officer and Co-founder at NaviGate. “Seeing it run in orbit without a single anomaly, and produce solutions consistent with the reference orbits computed on the ground, is the validation we were working toward, and a real milestone for the whole NaviGate team. D-Orbit’s Software In-Orbit Demonstration service was key to getting there quickly: we developed and tested our application on the ground in the same containerized environment used in orbit, iterated fast, and flew on real flight data within months, which is exactly what a company like ours needs to bring a flight-proven product to market.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “With five networked Intelligence Nodes in orbit, we can give customers access to space infrastructure that is already up and running. For NaviGate, that means testing their precise orbit determination algorithms ingesting raw GNSS measurements and attitude telemetry in real time from D-Orbit’s ION platform, in-situ directly on-board, with no satellite to develop or launch. It’s a practical way to move from simulation to real flight data in less time and at lower cost,” said Viney Jean-Francois Dhiri, Head of Growth, Sales and Marketing of the Space Cloud Business Unit at D-Orbit.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Caravel is the first release of the NaviCode fleet: subsequent versions will extend these capabilities to multi-sensor resilient navigation and to autonomous maneuver planning for large constellations. NaviCode Caravel was also selected as a winner of the CASSINI Challenges 2026, the European Union’s space entrepreneurship competition run by the EU Agency for the Space Programme (EUSPA).

The in-orbit demonstration is the culminating milestone of the proof-of-concept program funded by Galaxia, the Italian Technology Transfer Hub on Aerospace powered by CDP Venture Capital together with Obloo Ventures, which backed NaviGate from its earliest stage. NaviGate was founded by researchers who developed deep expertise in spacecraft navigation and precise orbit determination through their work on ESA and NASA missions, and originated as a spin-off of Sapienza University of Rome.

Following the demonstration, NaviGate is engaging constellation operators and mission integrators for the first pilot deployments. NaviCode Caravel addresses concrete needs across the market: reducing the ground workload and infrastructure required for precise orbit determination in constellation operations, enhancing onboard image processing for Earth observation missions, supporting PNT constellations, and improving orbit knowledge for launch vehicles and orbital transfer applications, with further applications across other mission types and orbital regimes.

articles.title: Galileo Space Is Building Satellites That Turn Signals Into Answers in Orbit
articles.author: Galileo Space

paras.en: Galileo Space is building satellites designed to turn signals into answers in orbit. Modern defense and commercial operations need fast answers about what is happening and where. Existing systems can leave segmented data crawling through processing for hours or days. FPV drones and moving radars must be detected and tracked quickly. Ballistic missile launch plume detection can provide critical early warning. Interference disrupting navigation frequencies or crucial satcom links must be detected and traced to its source. A ship lost at sea may still broadcast a distress signal. A tumbling satellite may lose contact with the ground while still emitting signals that help locate it. Rescue crews may have only hours to find someone before nightfall.

paras.en: The solution combines innovative sensors with AI fusion at the edge to generate actionable reports directly in orbit. The system is designed to operate fully autonomously for weeks, selecting and carrying out its own sensing tasks. It identifies threats, geolocates signals and delivers actionable intelligence to operators within minutes, not hours or days. The mission is to give defense teams the early warning they need to survive and commercial operators the answers they need to act.

Working side by side with government stakeholders, the team has developed a deep understanding of operational needs and critical capability gaps. The company is in the final stages of securing its first government contract. Its first demonstration satellite is scheduled to launch in Q4 of 2027 to prove its capabilities in orbit and open the door to a potential Phase III government contract. Galileo has also deepened relationships with commercial companies that need near live data, creating a path to early revenue alongside its defense business.

articles.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5016–5021: Fantastic Minerals and How To Detect Them

paras.en: Written by Lucy Lim, Planetary Scientist at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center
Earth planning date: Friday, Sept. 18, 2026

Curiosity surprised us at the beginning of the week with a change in rock texture — instead of the finely layered bedrock blocks we've been seeing in our recent sulfate unit workspaces, suddenly we were looking at blocks covered (and likely filled) with a jumble of small disc-shaped lumps. We've seen somewhat similar features before much earlier in the mission — for example, close to the Pahrump Hills back in the Murray mudstones, and they're sometimes seen in Earth rocks as well, especially in settings in which minerals were precipitating from an evaporating fluid. The disc-like shapes could be created by the growth habits of a specific crystalline mineral that is known to grow into similar shapes, or they could be bits of a harder rock layer that broke up and collected here. We planned Mastcam and MAHLI imaging for more morphological detail on the jumbled disc blocks (“Yungay,” “Chiu Chiu”) as well as LIBS (“Puya Raimondii,” “Liolaemus Tacnae,” “Pisqu Warkatana”) and APXS (“Salar de Vacas”) to investigate their composition.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Ongoing long-distance imaging projects were furthered by ChemCam long-distance remote imager (RMI) and Mastcam mosaics of the buttes on either side of Valle Grande. These “cutaway”-view images of the strata above the rover will help us map sedimentary structures in these upcoming units and understand how these rocks formed and eroded. Views of more recent erosional deposits will also help us to understand the formation of Valle Grande itself.

In order to identify minerals, Curiosity needs data from the CheMin X-ray diffraction instrument, which means a drill campaign. We've driven over a kilometer since our last drill site at Campo Marte, and this will be our first drill above the erosional supersurface. The Wednesday plan's drive brought us up next to a promising drill workspace a little beyond where we saw the disc-shaped features discussed above (imaged as “Torres del Paine” by Mastcam) and Friday’s planning included site characterization with the instruments on Curiosity's arm (“Alberta Wild Rose,” “Moonraker Mountain”), ChemCam LIBS (“Osoyoos”), and Mastcam (“Trincomali Channel,” “Yellow Lady's Slipper”). The team also selected a specific drill target and planned a very short drive to bring it in range of the arm — first for contact science and then, if all goes well, for the preload test and drill.

articles.title: An Agricultural “Island” in the Saskatchewan River Delta

paras.en: Much of the Saskatchewan River Delta, a large inland delta that straddles the Canadian provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba, is too wet for extensive farming. But amid the delta’s winding channels, lakes, and marshes, an “island” of straight-edged fields breaks up the curvy contours. These fields, west of the town of The Pas, make up Manitoba’s northernmost agricultural area.

Known as the Carrot River Valley (Pasquia Area Settlement), the area lies within the Rural Municipality of Kelsey. Its actively farmed land spans more than 40,000 hectares (100,000 acres) between the Carrot and Pasquia rivers—tributaries of the Saskatchewan River—and is surrounded by wetlands, including the marshes of the Saskeram Wildlife Management Area to the north.

These images show the valley at two points during the 2026 growing season: on July 2 (left) and September 21 (right). They were acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on the NASA-USGS Landsat 9 and Landsat 8 satellites, respectively.

Landsat data feed into the Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada annual crop inventory. The 2026 inventory was not released as of late September, but the 2025 map shows that farmers in the Carrot River Valley grew mostly canola and spring wheat that year, along with small patches of Canary seed.

The July 2026 image shows green crops across many of the valley's fields. Planting in the area, part of Manitoba Agriculture’s Northwest crop reporting region, began later than in parts of the region to the south because of wet conditions. Still, fertile soils and long summer days at this northern latitude can help crops grow quickly.

By the time of the September image, the pattern had flipped. The Pas recorded little rainfall in the preceding week (1.6 millimeters, or 0.06 inches), while wetter weather elsewhere in the Northwest region (up to 43.9 millimeters, or 1.7 inches) held up the harvest. By then, farmers across the region had harvested about 10 percent of the canola and 50 percent of the spring wheat.

Managing water has long been a challenge in the valley. In the 1950s, a major flood control and drainage project got underway, and farming in the area today still depends on diking and pumping for agricultural flood protection.
NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey. Story by Kathryn Hansen.

articles.title: APOD: 2026 October 1 – Harvest Moon with Erupting Mount Etna

paras.en: Explanation: Have you ever seen the full moon rise? This colorful image was photographed last weekend in Sicily, just outside the town of Nicosia, in Italy. It is a composite photograph that shows the Moon rising as the sky turns darker. Lower clouds are reflecting the colors of antitwilight, while ash and gas from Mount Etna are seen higher in the background. The pink band lower in the sky is called the Belt of Venus. During a full moon, the Moon and the Sun are in opposition in the sky: the moon rises as the sun sets. The lunar phase cycle lasts approximately 29.5 days (but the Moon takes approximately 27 days to orbit the Earth). In some cultures of the Northern Hemisphere, the September full moon is called the Harvest Moon. Does your culture have a special name for it? (A full moon by any other name would shine as bright.)

articles.title: Could a new global panel defuse inequality’s ‘ticking time bomb’?

paras.en: Could a new global panel defuse inequality’s ‘ticking time bomb’?

That is the thinking behind a proposal gaining support from world leaders and experts to establish a new ‘International Panel on Inequality’, an independent body that would bring together evidence on the causes and consequences of widening disparities and help governments understand what can be done about them.
The initiative was in the spotlight in New York on 23 September, at an event on the margins of the UN General Assembly’s high-level week, convened by Brazil, Norway, South Africa and Spain.

In remarks delivered by Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed, UN Secretary-General António Guterres cast the challenge in stark terms, warning of deepening concentrations of wealth and power and the risks they pose to societies and the international system.

“Sustainable Development Goal 10 calls on us to reduce inequality within and among nations. And yet we see breathtaking levels of income and wealth inequality, with the richest 10 per cent of the world’s population now owning 75 per cent of all wealth,” Mr. Guterres said.
For the Secretary-General, the concern is not simply the scale of inequality today, but how quickly it could deepen.
He warned that the rapid development of frontier technologies could make existing disparities considerably worse, particularly if their wealth and power remain concentrated in only a few hands.

“The breakneck emergence of frontier technology – and the concentration of this technology’s wealth and power in a tiny number of hands – could unleash global inequality at a scale far beyond anything that we have seen,” he said.

The consequences, he warned, reach beyond household incomes and individual opportunity. Unchecked inequality could undermine democratic institutions and deepen the imbalance of power between countries.
“A world where only a few powerful countries can exert control over global security and the global economic architecture is a ticking time bomb,” he said.
According to the UN chief, the proposed International Panel on Inequality would seek to place independent, science-based evidence at the heart of the global response.
It would bring together experts to analyse the scale, causes and consequences of inequality and identify practical policy choices available to governments.

Those options could include greater investment in education, health, social protection and decent work; fairer taxation; stronger international cooperation on development finance, trade and investment; reform of the global financial architecture; and more effective enforcement of rules governing corporations and high-net-worth individuals operating across borders.
Gender equality would be central to the Panel’s work, alongside efforts to ensure that technologies such as artificial intelligence are accessible to, and governed by, all countries.
“This proposed Panel can deepen our understanding of the problem – and the policy and political choices that we need to address it,” the Secretary-General said.

Nobel laureate economist Joseph Stiglitz, who chairs the founding committee behind the initiative, argued that inequality should be treated as a global challenge requiring the same depth of scientific analysis that climate change has received.

“Inequality within and between nations is a collective threat to the functioning of our economies and their ability to support human dignity,” he said, stressing that its effects extend well beyond economics to politics, societies and the environment.
The model is the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, or IPCC, which provides the comparison at the heart of the initiative.

Mr. Stiglitz said the proposed inequality panel would similarly provide an independent body of experts able to “assess, synthesize, and present trusted knowledge and analysis” on the causes and consequences of inequality and possible policy responses.
But he also stressed the importance of giving such a body a multilateral foundation and legitimacy. The founding committee, he said, supports establishing the Panel through a UN resolution.
Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley gave the proposal strong backing at the meeting, looking ahead to the possibility of action by the General Assembly.
For Ms. Mottley, tackling inequality goes to the heart of whether the international community can fulfil the promises made to people through the United Nations.

“I'd like to thank Brazil, Norway, South Africa, and Spain for convening this session that allows us to be able to tee up a resolution that I suspect will become a groundbreaking resolution for this body, recognizing that if we want to be able to guarantee the promise of the UN charter to our citizens across the world, it will be impossible for us to do without ensuring that we address this fundamental issue of income inequality,” said Ms. Mottley.

articles.title: World News in Brief: Storm clouds over Gaza, deadly obstacles face Mexican women rights defenders, Latvia booze ban proves lifesaver

paras.en: World News in Brief: Storm clouds over Gaza, deadly obstacles face Mexican women rights defenders, Latvia booze ban proves lifesaver

UN teams are racing to protect families in Gaza from the coming rainy season, but restricted access to land and shortages of critical supplies are hampering the effort, UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said on Wednesday.
Since Monday, partners have assessed three possible sites for temporary shelters for people choosing to leave flood-prone areas or war-damaged buildings at risk of collapse.
They are also examining more than 450 existing displacement sites at high risk of flooding – home to about a fifth of Gaza’s population.

Explosive ordnance must be cleared from the new sites before voluntary relocation can happen at scale, Mr. Dujarric said, along with levelling sandy ground and installing drainage, water and lighting.
“The main obstacle is restrictions on access to 65 per cent of Gaza’s land”, he said, adding that the remaining 35 per cent is already overcrowded.
More Israeli approvals are needed to import machinery, spare parts and engine oil, while funding for fuel and shelter is also urgently required.
Meanwhile, health partners are training local medical staff to manage non-communicable diseases, but medicine shortages are limiting early detection and treatment.
“Life-threatening gaps remain in specialized cancer care, including shortages of essential chemotherapy and radiotherapy supplies.”
Women searching for Mexico’s disappeared face deadly violence

Women searching for people forcibly disappeared in Mexico continue to face deadly violence and often themselves become victims, independent UN human rights experts warned on Wednesday, urging the State to protect them.

Recent attacks in Sinaloa highlight the risks. On 29 August, human rights defender Elisa Altagracia Bonilla was reported disappeared, and Alma Rosa Rojo Medina, founder of the collective Voces Unidas por la Vida, was attacked alongside her daughter and two children.
On 1 September, members of the collective Corazones Unidos por una Misma Causa were struck by a vehicle during a peaceful demonstration in Mazatlán.
The same collective has been repeatedly targeted: one member, Rubí Gómez-Tagle, was murdered this year, and another, María de los Ángeles Valenzuela, disappeared in October 2025.

“The work of these women constitutes a fundamental extension of their rights, the right to truth, justice and reparations…They are carrying out a task that is primarily the State’s responsibility. The State must fully assume this responsibility and not shift the burden onto the families,” the experts said.
The violence occurs amid near-total impunity, they added, calling it “a tragic example of the State’s failure to fulfil its obligations to protect human rights defenders”.

The independent experts – who are not UN staff and receive no salary for their work – welcomed the General Assembly’s decision to designate 19 December the International Day in Recognition of Women Searchers for Disappeared Persons, and urged Mexico to publicly recognise the importance of these women’s work.
They have previously raised their concerns with the Government, including in an April 2026 letter about the killing of Ms. Gómez-Tagle, to which it replied.
New alcohol policy gives booze the boot in Latvia
To Latvia finally, where simple public health measures to reduce alcohol consumption have been linked to a “significant decline in deaths”, just months after they took effect.
According to the UN World Health Organization (WHO), deaths that were wholly attributable to heavy drinking decreased by 27 per cent, after the new restrictions came into effect.

Mortality from alcohol poisoning, liver disease and acute pancreatitis that are all associated with regular drinking “fell significantly”, WHO noted, after evaluating data submitted by the Latvian health authorities.

Karina Zalite, head of WHO’s Country Office in Latvia, welcomed the Government’s measures to make alcohol less available, including reducing times when it can be bought, ending instant deliveries when it is purchased online and restricting promotions and sales in gambling venues:
“Alcohol is everywhere in our lives,” she noted.
“It’s at celebrations, in sport, at the checkout counters and stores. It’s easy to forget what it really is, an addictive substance and one linked to at least seven types of cancer.”
According to WHO, cancers associated with drinking include bowel cancer and breast cancer. Alcohol use is responsible for approximately 800,000 deaths across Europe every year.

articles.title: Who gets to shape AI? UN debate centres on power, trust and inclusion

paras.en: Who gets to shape AI? UN debate centres on power, trust and inclusion

Artificial Intelligence or AI – and the technology behind it – is moving fast. The question being asked across the world is who gets a seat at the table deciding how it's used and who gets to benefit.
When global leaders gathered at the UN during High-Level Week at the organization’s headquarters in New York, AI emerged as an issue which both unified and divided nations.
Although they largely agree there are significant upsides to AI, they are split on the risks, who writes the rules, and how to stop entire countries from being left behind.
UN News reviewed some of the key speeches made during the UN General Debate to get a sense of the challenges and benefits that nations are focused on.
As UN Secretary-General António Guterres put it: “AI is indeed a game changer — with enormous promise to advance medicine, accelerate scientific discovery, expand opportunity, and improve lives.”
Countries seemed focused on finding the right balance: How can we push the positive aspects of AI technology forward without opening the door to disaster at the hands of rogue agents?
President of the General Assembly Khalilur Rahman put it plainly: “AI can be a powerful accelerator of human progress; therefore, we must not close the door to innovation.”
But he also flagged the potential harms; job losses and deepening digital divides while calling for guardrails grounded in science, not fear.
Switzerland struck a similar note, warning that regulation needs to build trust without choking off AI's benefits. Japan zeroed in on cooperation over frontier AI safety.
Saudi Arabia leaned into ethics and responsible use. Singapore backed testing, trust-building and cross-border incident reporting, while flagging the dangers of increasingly autonomous systems.
Mr. Guterres framed the challenge starkly: “The danger is not technology. The danger is technology without accountability: Capability without oversight. Decision-making without transparency.”
Once the policy talk is stripped away, most countries are asking: what does this mean for daily life?

The UK talked up faster cancer diagnoses, economic renewal and better public services. India went further, describing AI as a ground-breaking development tool: “We view AI as a transformational driver, for human empowerment, economic prosperity and population-scale problem solving.”
The UK also focused on the potential disruptions. “But we know that AI will also be a source of disruption to the way we live and work, and a multiplier of risk.”

The solution? Keep humans, specifically, elected ones, in charge: “Fundamental decisions on this technology are too important to be left to chance. They must be taken by elected governments who serve working people.”
These concerns reflect a broader debate over whether AI will shrink or deepen inequality.
Another recurring question was whether countries will merely use AI or help shape its future.

South Africa was direct: Africa needs a hand in writing those rules, tying it to research, youth and economic transformation. Switzerland agreed that real participation means shaping governance, not just getting access.

India pushed for sovereignty: "We believe in the right of each nation, to shape its eco-system, with the development of its own models, and deployment strategies, consistent with its national goals and priorities."
Meanwhile, China focused on ensuring that technological advances are shared broadly rather than concentrated among a few countries or societies.
“We should take a people centered approach and develop AI for the positive and for good, narrow the digital divide and promote development that is universally beneficial.”
Singapore went further still, floating the idea of a future UN framework convention and a dedicated international AI institution, with everyone, not just the frontrunners, at the table.

The UN has already started bringing countries together to discuss the issues raised by AI including establishing an Independent International Scientific Panel on AI and holding a Global Dialogue on AI Governance
The concentration of data, computing power and influence remains a significant worry for many nations.
Brazil flagged the outsized sway of big tech companies. France raised the risk of dependence on either dominant States or a handful of private firms.

Developing countries want to play a bigger role in digital development, urging more access to increased computing power, technical know-how, infrastructure, and a significant say in setting standards.
China tied this to the digital divide, South Africa to participation in research and governance, Saudi Arabia to capacity-building institutions and Switzerland to skills and infrastructure support.
The takeaway: The future of AI may be as much about access as it is about regulation.
Security concerns emerged through plenty of speeches.
- France flagged risks around defence, cybersecurity and space.
- Japan pointed to information integrity and increasingly powerful frontier systems.
- Türkiye called for an international legal framework.
- Ukraine warned that the more capable this technology gets, the more urgent the search for peace becomes.
- Singapore added its voice to worries about autonomous weapons and the loss of human control.
While many nations favour the idea of cooperation, finding common ground on how far it should go, remains problematic.

Russia backed UN-centred rulemaking with universal buy-in. Türkiye pushed for work on a UN convention on AI. The UK called for global principles and standards, and said AI will be a headline issue when it takes the G20 presidency.

The UN chief went furthest, laying out concrete proposals including stronger safeguards, independent oversight, a new risk-management architecture: “But because this affects us all, global coordination is indispensable,” he told the General Assembly.
Not all sovereign governments are convinced tighter controls are the answer. The United States offered the sharpest counterpoint, treating AI dominance as a strategic and economic imperative.

President Donald Trump argued for an alternative vision: "I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution. Many say bigger than the Industrial Revolution or the Internet itself."

articles.title: A family affair! How Jack and Kevin Sinfield will live out fairy tale Grand Final moment

paras.en: Super League Grand Final will be a special family affair for Sir Kevin Sinfield and son Jack at Old Trafford

Sir Kevin Sinfield's son Jack Sinfield will play in his first Grand Final on Saturday and his dad will deliver the match ball; watch Warrington Wolves take on Wakefield Trinity in the Super League Grand Final on Saturday October 3, live on Sky Sports from 5pm
A Super League Grand Final week is special for anyone but it is a uniquely special moment for Jack Sinfield.

Sinfield is the son of Sir Kevin Sinfield MBE who is in the middle of his latest gruelling running endeavour, running seven ultra marathons in seven days stopping at all 12 English Super League clubs along the way.
Kevin Sinfield has helped raise more than £11m for the MND community with his team since his first annual challenge in 2020.
He will finish his final challenge by coming out to onto the Old Trafford pitch and delivering the match ball with his son, Jack, who will be gearing up to play in his first ever Super League final.
Wakefield take on Warrington Wolves to make history and become the sixth-ever Super League winner, live on Sky Sports on Saturday October 3.

All at once, the Wakefield man will have overwhelming pride in his dad, the nerves of the biggest moment of his career, and the pressure of trying to emulate all the wins on that hallowed turf that his dad pulled off with Leeds.
Jack Sinfield has been missing his dad while he has been away and knows you could not write the outcome that has happened with their journeys colliding at the Theatre of Dreams.

"I've spoke to him (dad) a little bit, but obviously he's been really tired. I think I've said already that when he planned this last challenge and for it to finish at Old Trafford, I don't think even he could have imagined that I would be playing in it. So it's worked out pretty well," Jack Sinfield said.
"It was really nice to see him. I've obviously missed him a lot when he's been away because I'm still living at home, so it's really weird around the house without him.
"I'm hoping I'll see him on Thursday when he goes past home and he runs up near our neck of the woods."
From childhood memories to career highlights: Emulating dad
Old Trafford is not a new place to Jack as he spent his childhood watching his dad, the Leeds Rhinos legend win the Super League on seven occasions.
He has cherished memories of his dad's career highlights and now knows it is his moment to try and "emulate" him.

"My first ever rugby league game was the 2004 Grand Final when I was three weeks old. I have been to every single one of the Grand Finals my dad has played in but the last one really stands out in 2015," he added.

"I had just turned 11 then so that's the one I really remember the most, knowing it was his last game as well. Obviously it was really emotional for us all as a family and that's the main memory I have that really sticks out, especially with it being the game where Leeds won the treble.

"I didn't realise how stressful it was trying to sort tickets, I've seen my dad do it for years. The last two days have been carnage trying to sort everything out. But it's worth it, these are the games you want to be playing in, so it's all worth it.
"It's been a dream of mine to go there one day and emulate him and win one. But now it's here, it's definitely feeling a bit different.
"I've got that picture on my phone still. It was a pretty special moment - hopefully there will be a chance to have another picture this weekend.. I'd want him to have a shower first though."

Indeed, the player of the match award is now called the Rob Burrow Award. Imagine the fairy tale if Sinfield senior watches his son win the trophy named after his mate who has inspired all the charity work he has taken on. Who inspired a sport. Who inspired a nation.
How to watch the Super League Grand Final
The Super League Grand Final takes place at Old Trafford on Saturday October 3, live on Sky Sports Main Event and Sky Sports+.
The match will take place at 6pm, with coverage on Sky Sports from 5pm.

articles.title: 'I find myself defending you!' - For how long will Fury-AJ stay friendly?

paras.en: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua: Rivals show respect at friendly first press conference - but how long will it last?

Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua will finally settle their rivalry in a British heavyweight blockbuster at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff on Friday December 11; Fury and Joshua both traded taunts at their first press conference in London; the British duo then shared a face-off
Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua finally came face-to-face on Wednesday - but few could have predicted how their first press conference ahead of their blockbuster heavyweight clash would unfold.

Perhaps because of the uncertainty that has continued to surround the fight since it was announced, there was something of a surreal atmosphere in west London until the two biggest names in British boxing finally appeared on stage shortly after 6pm.

The whole thing suddenly felt very real, with the audible excitement of the relatively small number of fans who had been able to buy tickets to watch from the arena's upper tier clearly appreciated by both fighters.

With the two-time world champions sat just a few feet apart, attention quickly turned to how they would interact after years of verbal sparring from a distance.
Joshua's measured persona made his approach easier to predict, but the wildcard was which version of Fury would show up.

After a lengthy introduction from master of ceremonies Max Kellerman, the American's questions about the fighters' sparring session - which took place in 2010, when Joshua was still an amateur - produced some light-hearted banter.

However, Joshua soon took control of the proceedings to pay tribute to several people in his life who had passed away, including Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Ayodele, who died in a car crash in Nigeria last December that Joshua survived.
Joshua requested a minute of silence which was impeccably observed by everyone in the arena, before applause at the end of it, which Fury warmly participated in.
Whether it had always been his intention or Joshua's words had influenced him, Fury then offered some extremely kind words about his rival.
"This man is a two-time heavyweight world champion, Olympic gold medallist, and he has been a role model and a poster boy for British boxing for years," Fury said.
"I mostly find myself defending my arch rival to fans I meet in the street. If you could achieve 10 per cent of what this man has achieved, you'd be doing well."

While there is little doubt tensions will rise and less friendly exchanges will follow between now and fight night, both fighters made it clear that there is a great deal of underlying respect between them, with no obvious personal malice.
That was further underlined when Fury invited Joshua to join him for a pint of Guinness in the pub after the fight, regardless of the result.
Joshua's humorous suspicion of the invitation, however, perhaps reflected his surprise at Fury's approach to the event. Was the master of mind games at it again?
Few are better qualified to analyse this event and everything around it than Britain's former undisputed heavyweight world champion Lennox Lewis, who was in attendance.
Lewis is adamant that once Fury and Joshua are deeper into their training camps, their exchanges will become less friendly.
"It's too early, at this time [for aggro]," Lewis said. "You need to be in training camp and not see people for a couple of weeks.
"To be training hard and thinking about each other. Then when they see each other, it will be different, because everyone will be touchy at that point."

Fury also showed just how quickly he can switch from friendly to confrontational when responding to a video released by Joshua and his promoter, Eddie Hearn, before the fight was finalised. The video positioned Joshua as a 'landlord' coming to collect his money.
Fury suggested that the fact his name appears first on all the promotional material for the event proves he is the A-side of the fight.
"In the build-up to this fight, Eddie [Hearn] and AJ were talking about landlords, being the boss, being the 'guvnor', the rent man and all that," Fury said.
"When I look behind me, I only see one don and that's Fury vs AJ. Now you've come to get the rent and I ain't f****** paying because I'm No 1.
"I don't make a big thing about all that but we're going to walk out seeing Tyson Fury versus his opponent Anthony Joshua - an old dosser who works for me."
With several details still to be decided - including which fighter will walk to the ring first and be left waiting for his opponent - the battle of egos is only likely to intensify.
While the result is ultimately all that will matter, it will be fascinating to see the receptions these two legends receive in the build-up to December 11 and right through to the opening bell.
If the first press conference was anything to go by, Fury and Joshua are set to receive a huge reception wherever they go between now and fight night.
After the huge cheers that greeted both fighters as they arrived on stage, Fury's fans broke into his "get up" catchphrase, with Joshua playfully joining in and repeating it back to them.
It was also notable that there was little of the hostility often directed at one fighter by the other's supporters. Instead, the focus was firmly on backing their respective heroes.
Joshua remained on stage for at least 30 minutes after the press conference had finished, signing autographs and posing for photos with fans.

After protracted negotiations had left the British public tired of waiting, this ultimately felt like a day of celebration for everything the pair have achieved in setting up one of the biggest fights in the sport's history.
The question now is: how long will the feel-good factor last?

articles.title: 'Could be in the first round' - AJ plots 'spectacular' win over Fury

paras.en: Anthony Joshua predicts first-round knockout against Tyson Fury amid hopes of producing 'spectacular' victory

Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua will finally settle their rivalry in a British heavyweight blockbuster at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff on Friday December 11; Fury and Joshua both traded taunts at their first press conference in London; the British duo then shared a face-off
Anthony Joshua said he wants to deliver a "spectacular" victory over Tyson Fury as he predicted the blockbuster heavyweight clash could end with a first-round knockout.
The pair came face to face on Wednesday in London for the first time since the long-awaited all-British clash was confirmed for December 11 in Cardiff.

The fight between the pair of two-time world champions, which has been a decade in the making, appeared to be in danger of falling through amid a dispute over where it would take place, with Joshua and his promoter Eddie Hearn pushing for it to be in the United Kingdom.
- 'Blast AJ out of there!' - Best of Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua press conference
- Latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract on NOW
- Download Sky Sports app for expert analysis, video and more
Asked what the fight means to him, Joshua told Sky Sports News: "It meant a lot to me because of the fans. Bringing it to the UK meant a lot to me for the fans.
"And for me personally, as much as it is just another fight because I don't like to make too much of it - it's just what we do - it would be amazing to get the victory in spectacular fashion."
Joshua revealed that he wasn't necessarily willing to walk away from the fight if his push to have it staged in the UK had failed.

He said: "I wanted to do everything I could to make it happen and part of that was it being in the UK and we got that so we're here, but I wasn't completely willing to walk away from it because it still needed to go ahead.
"You just listen to the cries and the conversation of those people who love boxing and love competition.
"People who wanted it to be in the UK would have still been happy that it happened, but I think getting it here is the cherry and icing and everything that needs to be on top of the cake."
Fury has been installed as an early favourite by bookmakers for the fight, with the fact Joshua has been floored in the opening round of two of his last three fights undoubtedly a factor.
Joshua admitted that he has "vulnerabilities" but insisted he is "hard to beat" and not considering retirement regardless of the outcome of the fight.
Asked where he feels like he's at as a boxer, Joshua replied: "Durable, hard to beat, can show vulnerabilities, but makes it exciting for the fans at home.
"There's more to come. The Anthony Joshua journey doesn't end here."
On his opponent, Joshua added: "He performs to the level he's at as well, if I'm honest.
"He's versatile, and he's a good little mover around in the ring."
And as for what he expects to happen in the ring on December 11, Joshua said: "A knockout, if I'm honest with you. Could be in the first round."
Asked whether that's his gameplan, Joshua added: "Yeah, it is."
