articles.title: Pakistan says 22 fighters killed in air attacks on Afghanistan

paras.en: Pakistan has launched air attacks on Afghanistan, saying it targeted “camps and hideouts” used by armed groups in two locations and killed an estimated 22 fighters.
The announcement by Pakistan’s Ministry of Information on Thursday came as Kabul accused Islamabad of killing at least nine women and children in attacks on its Kunar and Helmand provinces.
- list 1 of 4Why is violence between Pakistan and Afghanistan recurring?
- list 2 of 4Afghanistan says 28 fighters killed as Islamabad, Kabul trade accusations
- list 3 of 4Pakistan, Turkiye edge closer towards joining Saudi war against Houthis
- list 4 of 4Suicide bombing in Pakistan’s Dera Ismail Khan kills at least 12 people
Al Jazeera could not independently verify the casualty claims.
Zabihullah Mujahid, the spokesman for Afghanistan’s government, said the strikes took place late on Wednesday and that at least nine people were killed and 11 others wounded.
In a post on X, he said the attacks on northeastern Kunar and southern Helmand destroyed three houses.
“We condemn this act and consider it an aggression and crime against all accepted principles,” he wrote.

The alleged attacks come amid an escalation in fighting between the neighbouring countries after three months of relative calm. Islamabad accuses Kabul of harbouring armed groups, including the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan, who stage cross-border attacks on its territory.
The Afghan government denies the charge and says the Pakistani attacks have targeted civilian homes, killing and wounding women and children.

articles.title: Mourners bury DR Congo official killed after defending Ebola response

paras.en: Mourners have gathered in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to bury a local politician who his party said was beaten to death after he defended the government’s Ebola response on the radio.
The funeral for Marie-Celestin Karondwa was held in the city of Butembo on Wednesday.
- list 1 of 3DR Congo begins Ebola vaccination trials for frontline health workers
- list 2 of 3DR Congo’s Ebola outbreak spreads to two new health zones, WHO says
- list 3 of 3Ebola cases surpass 8,000 as DRC struggles to control outbreak

Karondwa was attacked on Sunday at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hotspot in North Kivu province, according to his political party, the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDSP), which leads the DRC government. He died of his injuries at a local hospital.
“They beat him up and then set the house on fire,” his granddaughter, Sagesse Kavira, told The Associated Press news agency at the funeral.
The party said Karondwa was “an innocent victim for having defended the party’s position on the existence of the Ebola virus disease … and the threat it poses to the population”.
It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack, how many were involved or what motivated it.

The killing follows a series of attacks on health workers and other responders as the Central African nation battles its 17th and deadliest Ebola outbreak, which has so far recorded more than 8,000 cases, including nearly 4,000 deaths.

The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, for which there is no vaccine or specific treatment, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Researchers are testing potential candidates, the agency said.
The WHO said Ebola was present in provinces including Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Sud Ubangi and Tshopo. It said Ituri remained the most affected.
Officials have tried to fight the outbreak through a village-based approach, but some residents have resisted, dismissing Ebola as a hoax amid deep distrust of the government.
Many believe the disease is a ruse for officials to siphon off money. Some refuse to report their symptoms due to disbelief or shame surrounding being an Ebola patient.
Responders say the scepticism has complicated their work, including in remote communities and newly emerging hotspots that are short of medical supplies and health workers.

The mistrust has been especially hard to overcome in rebel-held areas of eastern DRC, where decades of conflict and human rights abuses have left many residents wary of outsiders and state authorities.
Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO’s director general, has said the country’s east faces “a catastrophic collision of disease and conflict” hampering the response.

articles.title: Modi’s India takes on Trump more openly, from ‘terrorism’ to tariffs

paras.en: New Delhi, India — Speaking at an event in New York this week, India’s Foreign Affairs Minister S Jaishankar offered a blunt assessment of Washington: It has been an insensitive partner to India’s concerns over “terrorism”; has warmed to its arch-rival Pakistan; and has pursued “self-centered” trade policies that have disproportionately hurt the Global South.
That tone marks a new edge in how New Delhi is dealing with US President Donald Trump’s administration in Washington, analysts say, on the back of rising bilateral tensions between the capitals.

For decades, India has dealt with divisive issues with otherwise friendly nations quietly behind the scenes, away from spectacle. That has especially been New Delhi’s approach with Washington, where the relationship has broadly enjoyed wide bipartisan support.
However, after months of tensions, New Delhi is adopting a more openly critical tone towards Washington to address the volatility and uncertainty that Trump brings to the White House.

The changing tune in New Delhi also comes at a critical time for Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who faces mounting domestic pressure and criticism from the opposition for allegedly bowing down to US pressure, time and again. On Wednesday, Modi held a telephone call with Trump, which the Indian PM called “productive” — a cold and formal depiction far removed from his description of the US president as a “good friend” in previous years.

Chietigj Bajpaee, a senior research fellow for South Asia at the Chatham House think tank, said that Jaishankar’s remarks “offer a frank assessment” on the current state of the India-US relationship. “Clearly, the shine has come off the bilateral relationship after India was initially among the most optimistic about a second Trump term,” he said.
Jaishankar addressed frictions between India and the US while speaking at an Asia Society event after the UN General Assembly in New York ended on Monday.

“If I stand back and look at the [India-US] relationship, I note that much of the world has had a more difficult relationship with the US,” he said. “I mean that may not be a consolation, but that’s a reality.”

Trade has been one of the flashpoints. Washington is India’s largest trading partner, with bilateral goods trade reaching $149.1 billion in 2025; but the relationship remains tilted towards India with a $58.4 billion goods surplus.
Jaishankar started by noting: “Countries should not be so self-centred that you’re in your own world and take your decision and say, ‘Well, it was not my intention to make your life difficult’.”
The minister was partly referring to the economic spillover of the wars in Iran and Ukraine, urging that “sound common sense” should ensure that the basic needs of countries were not neglected.

But then, he referred to the trade negotiations between India and the US, that have so far yielded a roadmap to a deal — but not a deal itself. “Apart from the per capita gap between India and the United States, the nature of production and the nature of society is very different,” he noted.

The agricultural sector has been among the most contested points between the two, where India has kept its market largely closed for decades to safeguard its farmers. “The expectation that it could rapidly move forward was tested against the ground reality, which was much more complex,” he said, adding that “there is more or less an understanding on the trade agreement.”

At one point, India was among the countries facing the worst tariff rates imposed by Trump. After the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s sweeping tariffs in February, his administration swiftly turned to other tools, including a new 10 percent global tariff. Earlier this month, Trump signed a law under which the US can impose up to 100 percent tariffs on countries like India that purchase Russian oil.

Jaishankar pointed to these changes, noting that the negotiations created “bumps last year for the relationship,” and added that once the deal is closed, it “would contribute to a better relationship.”

Ajay Bisaria, a retired diplomat who served as high commissioner to Canada and Pakistan, and as ambassador to Poland, told Al Jazeera that with Washington, in particular, “India has decided to be more public because there has been a lot of public criticism and a sentiment that the US is bullying India and India has been silent.”

The new 100 percent tariff on India, due to come into effect in less than a month, “is sort of a deal breaker in the relationship right now,” said Bisaria. “If that becomes reality, then all Indian efforts [to reach out to the US] would come under scrutiny.”

But trade isn’t the only challenge in the relationship. A major rupture emerged in May last year, when New Delhi engaged in a four-day war with its bitter neighbour, Pakistan, after an attack by armed fighters in Indian-administered Kashmir killed 26 civilians.

New Delhi was upstaged as President Trump announced a ceasefire, claiming that he threatened both countries with economic damage if they didn’t stop fighting. For India, any question on Kashmir is strictly bilateral with Pakistan, with no room for so-called third-party intervention.

Nevertheless, Trump has gone on to claim dozens of times that he brokered the crucial ceasefire — as recently as at the UNGA in New York — that halted the war between two nuclear-armed neighbours. India took offence to these claims.

On the other hand, Pakistan’s leaders cozied up to Trump, showered high praise, and nominated him for a Nobel Peace Prize. Since then, the relationship between Islamabad and Washington has bloomed, to New Delhi’s obvious irk.
For India, Jaishankar said, “particularly important is the issue of terrorism.”

“As a country, perhaps there are very few countries which have been subjected to the kind of terrorism that we have from a neighbour as part of a deliberate, conscious policy over many, many decades,” Jaishankar said, referring to Pakistan.

“Now, if something which matters so deeply to us, there isn’t enough understanding or appreciation or empathy of that, I think that creates a problem too,” he said, adding that India’s primary concerns are “not fully appreciated” by its partner, the US.

New Delhi’s changing tone while addressing Washington “is a lesson learnt from its experiences,” said Bisaria, the former diplomat. “After the ceasefire issue, the moods changed — and it all became worse.”

Harsh Pant, vice president of the Observer Research Foundation, a New Delhi-based think tank, said that “the obsession with Pakistan in the Trump administration without taking India’s sensitivities into account contributed to the sense that, look, we need to start articulating it.”
“When at the top level, you don’t see reciprocity, then calculations change and decisions are taken to bring differences out in the open,” Pant told Al Jazeera, referring to Jaishankar’s comments.

Indians have been the biggest beneficiaries of the US’s H1B programme which allows hiring of foreign workers with training in specialty fields. But that has come under fire from Trump, under whose watch Washington has raised barriers and fees for applicants, amid growing criticism of the scheme from supporters of his MAGA movement.

“For many years, mobility was seen as an economic gain. Today the economics of mobility and the politics of mobility are at odds with each other, at least in some quarters,” Jaishankar said, referring to Trump’s anti-immigration politics.
“That certainly in public perception is an issue,” the minister said.

Domestic pressure appears to be finally catching up in New Delhi. “Modi is feeling domestic pressure, with key state elections coming up next year, especially amid some anti-incumbency,” said Bisaria. “It dictates that the government’s posture should not be one of taking bullying from the US.”

Pant said issues like migration impact the general public in India, with the world’s largest population. For years, such connections made the US “an attractive partner for a large mass of Indians.” But today, he said, ”the same issues are becoming a negative drag on the relationship.”
“The public mood in India is also changing perceptibly towards the US. And I think the government is articulating that negative sentiment now publicly,” Pant said.

When Trump returned to the White House for his second presidential run, many in New Delhi’s strategic community were optimistic about bilateral relations, because of the US president’s warm personal relations with PM Modi during his first term.
But things unravelled in the coming months.
Still, Chatham House’s Bajpaee said that despite widening divisions between the US and India, “both have not given up on reviving their relationship”.

He pointed to Jaishankar’s remarks that India isn’t singled out in having a difficult relationship with the US. “Rather, the downturn in India-US relations is a reflection of the Trump administration’s transactional and often unpredictable or erratic foreign policy,” he told Al Jazeera.
“This offers a potential off-ramp for an eventual reset in relations. The conclusion of a bilateral trade agreement is a key watchpoint for this,” Bajpaee added.
For New Delhi, Pant said, “it is now just the question of waiting Mr. Trump out.” Though he added, with a laugh, that India is not alone in that queue.
“Everyone is waiting him out. President Trump has little respect for conventions and norms of inter-state behaviour. How do you just deal with that individual?” Pant said.

articles.title: How Ukrainians are coping with new, more deadly Russian attacks
articles.author: Dave Davies

paras.en: How Ukrainians are coping with new, more deadly Russian attacks
Zanny Minton Beddoes, The Economist's editor in chief, just visited Ukraine. She says, despite all its drone weaponry, Kyiv is under extraordinary bombardment, as Russia tries to make it unlivable.

This is FRESH AIR. I'm Dave Davies. Since Russia invaded Ukraine 4 1/2 years ago, Ukrainian forces have held their own on the battlefield with support from Western allies, and morale among the country's civilian population has held up, despite punishing air attacks. But our guest, Zanny Minton Beddoes, editor in chief of The Economist, says the war is changing in ways that bring a new level of terror to Ukrainian citizens and pose serious threats to the country's economy.

Minton Beddoes recently returned from a reporting trip with a team of journalists to Ukraine, where, she says, both sides in the war are developing new weapons and refining tactics with lethal consequences. One example, so-called safari hunting drones that identify a person or vehicle as a target, then follow as the target flees in terror. The drone eventually dives and crashes into the target, detonating a deadly explosive charge. We've invited Zanny Minton Beddoes back on the show to talk about Ukraine and catch up on some other important topics, including the war with Iran, trade, tariffs and the state of U.S., European and Canadian alliances.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Zanny Minton Beddoes is a former economist for the International Monetary Fund who joined The Economist magazine in 1994. She holds degrees from Oxford University and Harvard University and is a regular commentator on television and radio. We recorded our conversation yesterday.
Zanny Minton Beddoes, welcome back to FRESH AIR.
ZANNY MINTON BEDDOES: Thank you so much for having me.

DAVIES: You and this team of journalists from the economist recently made an extensive trip to Ukraine. You've been there before. Why did you feel you wanted to make this kind of investment in this subject now?

MINTON BEDDOES: So you're right. I've been there four times since the invasion by Russia, the full-scale invasion - the first, I think, three weeks after the invasion, when I went to Kyiv and was the first journalist to interview President Zelenskyy. The reason I go is because I think this is the most important geopolitical conflict in Europe in, you know, the last 70 years. And I actually have a kind of personal soft spot for Ukraine. I lived there for a few months 30 years ago. I find it a fascinating country. And I - you know, I feel that you can only really understand something, particularly a conflict like that, if you actually see it close up.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And I have to say, Dave, this is a very sobering trip. And it was probably the most sobering since the very first time I went, which was, the first time, in 2022. The Russians were still just outside Kyiv. The city was virtually empty. You know, we went to see President Zelenskyy kind of in bunkers. And, I mean, it was in his palace, but there were sandbags everywhere. It really felt like a place at war. But the subsequent two times, when I went to Kyiv, it felt like a normal city. The war felt far away because the city then had very good air defenses. And, yes, there were occasional air alerts, but you felt as though you were in a very safe city.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: This time around, I went to Kyiv, and then I went to visit the brigade headquarters of one of the drone brigades, much closer to the front, in a location that I'm obviously not going to disclose, but much closer to the front. And Kyiv itself - and this is, I think, really important for people to understand - in the last couple of months, but really the last few weeks, has been under extraordinary bombardment from the Russians. And they are basically trying to make life unlivable in a city of several million people.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And there are two big things that have changed that have given the Russians an advantage. The first is that the Ukrainians have run out of interceptors for ballistic missiles, what are called PAC-3 interceptors produced by the U.S., which for the past couple of years have really helped them to defend themselves against ballistic missiles. And because these interceptors are in extremely short supply - they were used heavily in the Middle East recently in the Iran War - the Ukrainians have essentially hardly got any left. So the Russians are able to bombard the city at night with ballistic missiles.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And the second is that the Russians have made an innovation to their drones. Their kind of workhorse drone is something called the Shahed drone, which was originally made by Iran, that the Russians started producing at scale. And they have essentially attached jet propulsion to those drones, which makes them go much higher and much faster and thus makes them much harder for the Ukrainians to intercept. And Ukrainians had built sort of defensive drones that could intercept the Shaheds with a sort of 95% success rate. But now that they have these jet propulsion attached to them, that interception rate has gone down closer to 40%, and the Russians have enormous quantities of these drones that they are just sending into Ukraine, essentially, all day and all night now.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: DAVIES: What does that mean day to day for civilians who are used to air raid sirens, right? I mean, this is not like they're not used to living in a wartime.

MINTON BEDDOES: So I think the difference is that, you know - if you're living in Kyiv, you have an app on your phone. And I had it on my phone when I was there. And it goes off every time there is a you know, ballistic missile or a jet Shahed close - within, you know, a few, I think 50 or 100 kilometers. And basically, it's going off the whole time. And you are trying to live a normal life. And so you're looking, and you become normalized to this quite quickly, and you look at it and you say, well, is it likely to be in my part of town? Looks not too far away, so I'll - you know, if it's too close, you might go to a shelter. You might just keep an eye on it. But increasingly, it's happening all day, and you're suddenly discovering that the Metro isn't working. You're unable to get your kids from school. There's been an attack. A supermarkets blown up, you know. And every day, people are killed.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: DAVIES: You paid a visit to the operation center of an elite drone unit in the Ukrainian army. Share with us what you saw there.

MINTON BEDDOES: So Ukraine has several of these unarmed systems brigades, as they're called, which are units that specialize in drones. And they were set up often by civilians, technologists, sort of separate from the army structure, but they work with the army structure. And they are in the vanguard of what this war is about, particularly at the front lines. And it is very different from what you imagine, you know, warfare to be from the movies. A drone-based war is one where the actual front lines - there are no people visible. There is what Ukrainians call the kill zone, which is now something like 20 to 30 kilometers each way from the contact line, where, essentially, anything that moves will be shot down, shot at by a drone within seconds or minutes.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: MINTON BEDDOES: Yes, from both sides. There are hundreds of drones in the air - surveillance drones, drones, attack drones. That means that nothing can really move. So the few people who are there on both sides are, you know, in underground dugouts. They are often supplied by drone, or they're supplied by unmanned ground vehicles, essentially kind of robots on wheels. It's a dystopian hellscape. To be clear, I wasn't anywhere near there. I was sort of close to it, but well out of that area.

Then these drones are manned and sort of piloted by people in the brigade headquarters of the sort that I went to. They have huge screens, and it's like a cross between a sort of dystopian video game and a startup. There are huge numbers of computer screens. There are people who are plotting where the Russians - assets are. They are sending surveillance drones to go and find them. Then they're sending in drones to attack them. And the other side is doing that, too. And the area around the front line is now basically a sort of no-man's-land where nothing can move. And, you know, the Ukrainians are clearly trying to disrupt Russian supply lines by attacking well beyond the front lines. And then, of course, they're also increasingly hitting refineries much further into Russia. So this is a - on both sides, a drone-based war, whose characteristics are very, very fast innovation.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: DAVIES: And I mentioned in the introduction, these so-called safari drones, where a pilot located somewhere is looking at what the drone sees. They identify a target - might be a person, might be a vehicle - and essentially kind of track them from the air as if they're a safari hunter and then smash the drone into the target, blow up a charge, right?

MINTON BEDDOES: That's exactly - and that's what happens on the front line in this kill zone the whole time. What is sort of newer is that the Russians are doing the same thing to attack civilians in front-line towns, and increasingly and alarmingly, they have the capability to reach bigger cities, potentially Kyiv, with this kind of drone, too. So the notion of safari-hunting individuals to kill them is now no longer some sort of dystopian fantasy. It's something that can happen.

DAVIES: The dreadful video that I've seen of a man, who - and there's this drone buzzing around above him, you know, six or eight feet in the air, and he's dodging around, trying to get behind a truck to kind of avoid it. And eventually, the drone dives into him, and he wasn't killed, but he was seriously injured. But just seeing it just seems - is utterly terrifying.

MINTON BEDDOES: It is. And what was really sobering to me is it was tough enough seeing all of this at this sort of center of this war. But what I realized is that these are tactics and capabilities that can be used by the Russians elsewhere. And if you remember just a few weeks ago, there was a narrow escape at Leipzig Airport when there was an attack, which - a drone was attacking a cargo plane at the airport. It was foiled, but it was in Germany, and the German government has said that the Russians were behind it. And I think there was realization for me, and in one of the conversations I had with the senior people at this drone brigade - became clear to me that their view is, these are the capabilities that the Russians have. Don't think that they're going to be confined just to Ukraine.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And I think there is a growing concern amongst European politicians and intelligence services that there will be more of this. We've had alarms raised from the Polish government. We've had alarms raised from Balkan governments. We've had alarms raised across the board that the Russians may well be planning to do more of this. And what became clear to me is that it is technologically totally doable now.

DAVIES: We need to take a break here. Let me reintroduce you. We are speaking with Zanny Minton Beddoes. She is editor in chief for The Economist. We'll continue our conversation in just a moment. This is FRESH AIR.
(SOUNDBITE OF LOS SUPER SEVEN SONG, "CALLE DIECISEIS")

DAVIES: This is FRESH AIR, and our guest today is The Economist's editor in chief, Zanny Minton Beddoes. We're looking at the war in Ukraine, and we'll be discussing some other topics, including the conflict in the Middle East and the state of Western alliances. Our interview was recorded yesterday.

You know, the Ukrainians have been effective in sending drones, behind the lines in Russia and attacking, you know, military infrastructure, energy infrastructure. And one of the ways that they have been able to operate it is by using these Starlink satellite hookups, which are, you know, operated by SpaceX, Elon Musk's company. I understand that Musk does not let Ukraine use those for attacks inside Russia. Is that right?

MINTON BEDDOES: Yes, that's right. Starlink is available to the Ukrainians over Ukrainian territory, including the territory that is Ukrainian, but the Russians are occupying. But it is not available to them over Russia. And what that means is that the Ukrainians lack the ability to go after the launch sites, for example, for ballistic missiles. So there is a huge plea from the Ukrainians to the Americans to basically push SpaceX to allow them to have access to Starlink over Russian territory so that they can go after the launch sites from which these ballistic missiles are raining down on them.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Interestingly and alarmingly, something that I hadn't really focused on until I went to Ukraine and sort of really delved into this, the Russians have been and are building their own version of Starlink called Rassvet, which is still in its early stages. I think they put a couple of dozen or so satellites into space, nowhere near as many as Elon Musk has with SpaceX. But nonetheless, this capability is growing, and most people think that sometime in the next year or so, the Russians will have some Starlink equivalent, which will mean that they will be very easily able to direct and monitor drones going anywhere over Ukrainian territory, which will be another big blow to the Ukrainians.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: DAVIES: And if the Ukrainians haven't had access to the Starlink system in Russian territory, how have they been able to manage these attacks on Russian facilities?

MINTON BEDDOES: I mean, there are other ways of guiding, but they're not as good as Starlink. The Ukrainians are incredibly innovative. And I think the important thing for people to understand is that thus far, Ukraine has sort of been ahead of the Russians in drone innovation, and they've been amazing at building up this drone industry. They've been always in a sort of cat-and-mouse game, somewhat ahead of the Russians. The Russians have been able to scale up. They're, you know, a bigger economy. They're good at scaling up their innovations. And what's slightly alarming now is it seems as though the Russians are actually ahead on innovation as well as an ability to scale.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: I have no doubt that the Ukrainians will come up with new innovations, both in defensive drones and other areas. The question that is more uncertain right now is, do they have the financial capability and financial support to scale those innovations? And that's what really matters right now, because the truth is that Ukraine is very, very dependent on financial support. Unfortunately, there's no support coming from the U.S. anymore. When the Trump administration came in, the - until then, there had been a lot of support from the United States. Now there is really essentially none. Ukraine is financed by the Europeans, and the question is whether the Europeans will step up the pace of their financial support such that the Ukrainians have the money to scale up their drone program, which is essential to defend themselves.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: DAVIES: Yeah. I want to talk more about that in a moment. But I also wanted to just note the level of Russian casualties in this war. It seems that the Ukrainians have been able to inflict terrible punishment on the Russian forces, right?

MINTON BEDDOES: The level of casualties are just extraordinary, something on the order of 40,000 people a month - Russians - killed and wounded. This is an unfathomable number of people. But one thing that's important to remember is we've been talking about all of the ways in which Russia is bombarding Ukraine. But Ukraine is, you know, essentially holding the front line and actually making a few gains in certain places.

So the sort of overall picture of this war is that the Ukrainians have held off the Russians. The front lines have been basically stable. The Russians, at incredible cost - 40,000 people a month - I mean, it just - you know, and you can't - it's hard to imagine those numbers. And they're still not able to really make a lot of progress. In some areas, they're gaining a tiny bit of ground. In some areas, they're losing. But basically the front lines are stable. So what the Russians have decided to do, particularly in recent weeks, knowing that they are not making serious progress at the front line, is to try and break the morale of Ukrainian civilians by completely bombarding the cities.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: DAVIES: You know, there's a graph that you have in the article that came from your trip. It's a bar graph that shows, by year, how much money the Western allies have contributed to Ukraine's defense, and they're color-coded. You know, so much for the EU, so much for the United States, so much for other countries. And it was stunning to look - and I think it's in 2025 that the U.S. portion disappears. I'm not sure that much of the United States realizes that U.S. support for Ukraine has vanished completely.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: MINTON BEDDOES: Yep. There is essentially no financial support for Ukraine from the United States. To the extent that there is any weaponry going, it is weaponry that is being bought by the Europeans on behalf of the Ukrainians from the U.S. When - you know, when President Trump came in, it became very clear that he did not intend to continue supporting Ukraine, and that has happened completely. And I don't think that's that well-known. And what is even less well-known is the degree to which the Europeans have stepped up and basically are single-handedly supporting Ukraine.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Now, this is because it's also, of course - it's our continent. It's in our own interest as Europeans to do that. But I am very clear, having just been there, that the situation is very, very stark right now and that I don't think the rest of the world has realized the degree that Russia is attacking civilians - there's no simpler way, no other way of putting it - attacking civilians and civilian life - and that, in order to be able to survive that and mount a defense, the Ukrainians need faster and more financial support so that they can scale up their defensive capability and so that they can survive. And this country has been extraordinarily resilient in the last 4 1/2 years. And yet it looks to me more difficult than it has for a long time in this war...
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: MINTON BEDDOES: ...Without financial support.

DAVIES: One of the issues is - is Zelenskyy still trusted as a leader? I mean, there have been some corruption cases. There are pieces of legislation in the legislature which have not been adopted. What's your sense of Zelenskyy's leadership and to what extent his credibility is undermining the kind of support either in the country or among allies?

MINTON BEDDOES: So I think there is growing frustration politically within Ukraine with President Zelenskyy and his leadership. I think that's - in some ways, that's kind of normal after 4 1/2 years of war. There is corruption in Ukraine, undoubtedly. The anti-corruption unit, which has been set up and is funded by the European Union as an important part of the prerequisites that Ukraine has to have to eventually become a member of the European Union - this organization is effective, is powerful, is unearthing corruption. There is corruption in the highest echelons of government around - or at least there are accusations of it in the highest echelons of government.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: You know, this makes it more difficult. And as you say, Parliament - the Ukrainian Parliament has not passed some elements of some laws that the Europeans would like them to have passed as part of the sort of cleaning up of Ukraine. So that's very frustrating for the Europeans. It's not a perfect political situation.

On the other hand, this is a country fighting for its existence. And I'm not sure that this is as much a story of terrible corruption in Ukraine as it is a good-news story of the effectiveness of an anti-corruption unit shining a spotlight. And I see it as a sort of - a good sign that they're unearthing this and that they are, you know, shining the light on corruption where it is. And that's all part and parcel of Ukraine becoming more and more like the, you know, part of Europe that it should be.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But it's very difficult right now. You know, there should have been elections. Were it not for the war, there would have been elections. President Zelenskyy has been president a long time. In any country, he definitely is not someone who is so focused on institutional reform as he should be. There are huge shortcomings to elements of what President Zelenskyy does. But I wouldn't conclude from that that, you know, it's a terribly corrupt place, and therefore, we shouldn't support it. I think it's remarkable what the Ukrainians are doing, given what they're facing.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: DAVIES: All right. We're going to take another break here. We are speaking with Zanny Minton Beddoes. She is editor in chief for The Economist. She'll be back to talk more after this short break. I'm Dave Davies, and this is FRESH AIR.
(SOUNDBITE OF BELA FLECK, EDGAR MEYER & MIKE MARSHALL'S "TRAVIS")

DAVIES: This is FRESH AIR. I'm Dave Davies. We're speaking with Zanny Minton Beddoes, editor in chief of The Economist. We're discussing trade tariffs, the economic impact of the war in Iran and Russia's war with Ukraine. Minton Beddoes just returned from a reporting trip to Ukraine, where she conducted interviews and visited the operations center of an elite drone unit in Ukraine. We're also looking at the state of U.S. relations with our longtime allies, including Europe, Canada and the United Kingdom. We recorded our conversation yesterday.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: All right. Well, let's talk about some other things going on in the world, starting with the conflict in the Middle East. President Trump says the U.S. controls the Strait of Hormuz, and plenty of oil is flowing. The reality is somewhat different, right?

MINTON BEDDOES: Well, I actually think some oil is flowing through the Strait of Hormuz under the new arrangements that the U.S. military has put in place. Exactly how much is the matter of some debate, but there is certainly some oil flowing at greater cost. But that doesn't mean that we're back to where we were before the war. I mean, clearly, Iran is trying very hard to control the strait. Clearly, you now have the additional concern of what is happening with the Houthis, who are also trying to control another route out of the region. So there is lots of debate about just how much oil is getting out. But what's very clear, Dave, is that there isn't as much as there was before, and there certainly isn't refining product coming out as there was before. And that which is is much more expensive.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: DAVIES: Right, and prices remain very high. Do you see any prospect for a resolution of this conflict within the foreseeable future?

MINTON BEDDOES: Both sides say that, you know, there is a deal to be done, but that deal is the one on their terms. I think it seems to me unlikely that there is going to be a serious resolution anytime soon because Iran is determined to have a resolution much more on its terms, which President Trump is not willing to have. And Iran - you know, the Iranian regime is showing that it has an incredible capacity to endure economic pain. And I think where we are now is we have a U.S. government that is convinced that the more it can tighten the economic screws on Iran, at some point, the Iranian regime is going to have to cave and come to a deal on U.S. terms. And we have an Iranian regime, which, of course, has several factions within it, of which at least the hard-liners are absolutely not - determined not to cave and have shown themselves willing to inflict incredible pain on their population.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: So my sense is that the likely outcome is some version of the status quo for a while. And then either President Trump decides that he's going to go and try and bombard them into submission, or we go back to the agreement that was, you know, temporarily reached a few months ago, which is much more advantageous to Iran.

DAVIES: There was a story a while back that the Saudis had asked Trump to bomb the Houthis, who are making gains against the Saudi-backed regime in Yemen, and that Trump thought about doing it but in the end didn't. I mean, the problem, of course, is that when you increase hostilities in one place, there's a reaction elsewhere. You know, the Iranians can attack American allies. And Trump's kind of in a box here, isn't he?

MINTON BEDDOES: I actually think that that was a very meaningful moment. That decision, you're right. It appears that the Saudis asked for help, and, you know, President Trump decided no. If you stand back from this, we may well find that however this war turns out, it ends up being a turning point in the U.S. relationship with the region. And this was the story we put on our cover last week and looked into in some detail. And let me explain why I think that. You know, what have we learned from this war now? First of all, we've learned that the Gulf countries which relied on U.S. bases for their security have found that, actually, having U.S. bases doesn't necessarily provide you with security.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: DAVIES: It can make you a target, right?

MINTON BEDDOES: It can make you a target. We found that there's been a huge use of U.S. munitions, which is going to have knock-on effects for U.S. security all around the world. And we've learned that probably going forward, you know, what U.S. bases remain in the region will have to be moved and probably put underground to be safe because we are now in this new drone-based warfare, which changes the calculus. articles.title: Greetings from Syria, where time seems to melt as a glassmaker braves scorching temps
articles.author: Emily Feng

paras.en: Greetings from Syria, where time seems to melt as a glassmaker braves scorching temps
Our world as journalists can move fast; every day there's breaking news from all corners of the world, and we scramble to stay on top of multiple threads of information each day.

That is why I loved watching this glassmaker just outside the historic Old City in Damascus. In 100 degree summer heat, he patiently shaped cup after glass cup in the blistering furnace in front of him, seemingly impervious to the temperature.

Time seemed to matter less than the process of melting and stretching the hot, melted glass. He made cups and oil jars and decorative lamps in a variety of jewel colors, using techniques and styles that have not changed for decades. Watching his craft reminded me to slow down and enjoy the moment, too.

Even though his shop was right on the edge of the Old City of Damascus, it was largely empty. Syria's nearly 14-year civil war has ended, but the economy is still struggling, while inflation has ratcheted up the cost of living in the last year. Even a glass can be a luxury for some.

articles.title: Swiss glaciers suffer another year of record ice loss
articles.author: Imogen Foulkes

paras.en: Swiss glaciers suffer another year of record ice loss

BERN, Switzerland — Switzerland's glaciers lost more than 5% of their ice in 2026, marking another year of rapid decline. The loss reflects a wider global trend: Glaciers around the world have been shrinking at increasingly rapid rates, a phenomenon scientists link directly to global warming.

Matthias Huss leads Switzerland's glacier monitoring network, known as GLAMOS, which released the report alongside the Swiss Academy of Sciences (SCNAT). Each summer, Huss heads high into the mountains to measure the country's ice fields. For years, his research has documented rapid ice loss, with the decline peaking in 2022, when Switzerland recorded a record 6% loss in a single year.
At the end of this year's long, hot summer, Huss returned to some of the glaciers to find much of the ice gone.
"They are completely devoid of ice," he said. "It's a moon landscape that is dry and dead. There are some little remnants, some ice blocks still lying around and melting there on the hot rocks."

In other places, alpine plants are now seeding themselves in areas once covered by glaciers that were meters thick. This year's glacier monitoring report shows the ice loss in 2026 is 5.5%, and the only reason it is slightly lower than 2022's record is because there was slightly more winter snow covering the ice.
Ominously, though, Huss' research shows that individual glaciers, among them Switzerland's biggest, like the mighty Rhône and Aletsch, have suffered record ice loss this year.

Why is this important? Because these huge ice fields are often called Europe's water towers. They store winter snow and release it gently as it melts over the spring and summer. That snowmelt fills Europe's key waterways, like the Rhine and the Danube. The water is key to Europe's food supply, and much more.

"It's the food supply, it's the transportation chains," says Huss. This summer, as river levels sank, freight transport in the Rhine and Danube came to a standstill, and nuclear power stations, cooled by river water, had to be temporarily shut down.

This situation can only get worse if the melt continues. Although Europe's rivers did have some water this summer, it came not from seasonal snowmelt, but from the glaciers themselves melting. Once they are gone — and 1,200 smaller glaciers have disappeared in the last 50 years — drought could pose an existential threat to Europe's farmers.

There are other threats too. Glaciers and alpine permafrost are key to stability; they are a kind of glue that holds the mountains together. Without that glue, the risk of landslides and even flooding increases. Last year, the Swiss village of Blatten was wiped out when a fragile glacier crashed down, bringing the side of the mountain with it and destroying 300 homes.

Fortunately, the instability was being monitored, and Blatten's population was evacuated before the landslide. But one year later, they are still living in temporary accommodation, with no idea if they will ever be able to return to homes now buried under an estimated 9 million cubic meters of ice, rock and mud.
This summer, on Nepal's border with Tibet, the collapse of a glacier triggered devastating floods that killed at least 1,400 people.

Matthias Huss is cautious about making a direct link between climate change and such disasters. Mountain environments, he points out, have always been risky. "It's a bit more complicated than just saying it's warm and the glaciers are disappearing, so the mountains are falling apart and causing disasters like this," he explains.

But, he adds, climate change can be the catalyst for such natural disasters. "Combined with this heat, with the disappearance of the ice, with the warming of permafrost, climate change can be a triggering factor. That can just be the last bit that is missing to trigger such events."

And after years of monitoring the glaciers, Huss has little patience with those who still claim climate change does not exist. What is happening to the glaciers should be a warning sign, he argues. "Look at them, it's not a hoax. The evidence is clear, and it's been clear for decades. And I think many people have understood that it's time to act now."

Without action, Europe's beloved alpine landscape could, quite soon, look very different. If the planet keeps warming at its current rate, the glacier monitoring unit predicts, all the glaciers will be gone by the end of this century.

articles.title: Atlanta Dream advance to WNBA playoffs semifinals for first time since 2018 with Game 2 win

paras.en: The Atlanta Dream avoided a first-round playoff exit for the first time in four years.

Atlanta, which finished with the Eastern Conference’s best regular-season record, had little trouble dispatching the Washington Mystics in Game 2 of their first-round WNBA playoff series Tuesday night. Star guard Allisha Gray led the Dream with 22 points in the 83-75 victory, punching Atlanta’s ticket to the semifinals for the first time since 2018.

Atlanta’s postseason run will continue Sunday, when the Dream host Game 1 of the semifinals against New York. The Liberty made league history by sweeping Minnesota, becoming the first No. 8 seed to eliminate a No. 1 seed in the league's 30-year history.

Jordin Canada made 3-pointers on back-to-back possessions in the fourth quarter, and she added a jumper from the free-throw line on Atlanta’s next trip for an 89-70 lead with just under three minutes left on the clock.

Rhyne Howard, the top pick in the 2022 WNBA Draft, ended the night with 15 points before fouling out with just over six minutes remaining in the fourth quarter. Angel Reese also had 15 points and seven rebounds.
The Mystics committed 11 first-half turnovers.
Washington went on a 14-2 run starting in the third quarter to get within 65-62. But Atlanta scored the next 13 points, capped by a 3-pointer by Canada, to rebuild a double-digit lead at 78-62.

The Mystics were making their first playoff appearance since winning the 2019 WNBA championship, while the Dream have captured the conference title three times from 2010-13 but have never won a WNBA championship.
The Dallas Wings hosted the Golden State Valkyries in Wednesday's other first-round series matchup.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: White Sox, Yankees advance to next round with sweeps as Munetaka Murakami provides quote of the year

paras.en: Wednesday afternoon had plenty of potential for drama, with all four wild card series offering the potential for teams to advance into the division round of the Major League Baseball playoffs.

The first game of the quadruple-header, the Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies, delivered in spades. A Bryce Harper misplay in the 7th inning allowed two Braves' runs to score, putting the Phillies on the brink of elimination. But Schwarber and Harper hit back-to-back homers in the 8th to tie it, and a 10th inning homer for Alec Bohm won it for Philadelphia to force a winner-take-all game three on Thursday.

Then there's the Houston Astros. The Astros entered game two needing a win to force a game three, sending their ace, Hunter Brown, to the mound against the White Sox' powerful lineup. 36 pitches, five hits, four runs, two errors and just two outs later, the White Sox had a 4-0 lead and Brown was out of the game.

That summed up Houston's series; just not quite good enough to overcome Chicago's offense. The White Sox, one of baseball's most strikeout-prone offenses, had 13 in Wednesday's game, but kept chipping away, fending off an attempted Astros comeback with a massive three-run homer from Chase Meidroth in the 6th inning to give them some breathing room.

Four combined innings from Jordan Hicks and Erick Fedde closed it out to send the White Sox through for a massive ALDS against their division rival Cleveland Guardians. But they weren't done with the entertainment quite yet.
In the postgame clubhouse celebrations, star first year third baseman Munetaka Murakami gave what might be the quote of the season. When asked how he felt, Murakami answered, "100."
A minute later, after being joined by another member of the White Sox staff, Murakami, covered in beer, added, "I'm drunk, I'm drunk. Yesterday, maybe hungover, you know?"
After the interviewer offered a gentle correction, he said, "No, not yesterday, tomorrow. Sorry, I don't speak English."

Meanwhile, on the other side of the American League postseason bracket, the New York Yankees had an opportunity to sweep the hated Boston Red Sox after a dominant 9-0 win in game one. And after Cam Schlittler's remarkable outing on Tuesday, Max Fried was nearly as good on Wednesday.

Six innings with just one run allowed, three hits, one walk and six strikeouts, enough for New York to take a 2-1 lead into the bottom of the sixth. Which is where everything imploded for Boston. Garrett Crochet, making his first appearance on a big league mound since late-April, took over, hoping to keep the Yankees at two.

Instead, Spencer Jones reached on a strikeout, then stole second and advanced to third on a throwing error from catcher Adley Rutschmann. George Lombard singled in a run, Jazz Chisholm poked one through the right side, Trent Grisham got a bunt down for a hit, knocking Crochet out of the game without getting an out. Garrett Whitlock came in to stop the bleeding, but after two more runs scored on a sac fly and groundout, Cody Bellinger delivered the big blow.
On a 1-0 changeup, Bellinger took advantage of the short right field porch and knocked in three to make it 8-1.
New York cruised home with a 9-2 win, setting up an ALDS matchup with the Tampa Bay Rays.

There are a few big takeaways from these two sweeps, namely the importance of power in October baseball. It's an old adage that small ball wins against quality pitching, but it was the homers from Chicago in game one and two that gave them the edge, while Bellinger's bomb effectively put the game out of reach in the Bronx. Even without Aaron Judge, the Yankees' lineup outscored Boston 17-2. And with two days off before the start of the ALDS, Schlittler will be able to start in game two of the ALDS, with Gerrit Cole or Carlos Rodon available for game one.

paras.en: While the Yankees are through, the other three teams left in the AL bracket are the Guardians, Rays and White Sox. Those teams rank 25th, 26th and 28th in total payroll respectively. There's a long ways to go to reach or win the World Series, but it's a bit of a tough look for MLB that the league office has spent the past few months preparing to lock players out by claiming that small market teams with low payrolls have no hope of meaningful baseball.
Pretty sure those three organizations should have hope. Saturday in Cleveland and Tampa should be a blast. Playoff baseball always is.

articles.title: Arizona sheriff's helicopter crew rescues man stranded atop overturned truck in rapidly rising floodwaters

paras.en: Dramatic video shows an Arizona sheriff's helicopter crew rescuing a man stranded on top of his overturned truck as rapidly moving floodwaters surrounded the vehicle.

The Maricopa County Sheriff's Office said its Fox 1 aviation crew responded Tuesday morning to a flooded wash in Tonopah, where deputies found the man sitting atop the overturned vehicle with water rushing around him.
Video released by authorities shows the man perched on the truck as muddy floodwaters rush past him.
Because of the dangerous conditions, first responders determined that directly reaching the man was too risky and decided a "hoist rescue" would be the safest option.
The video shows a Fox 1 crew member being lowered to the vehicle to secure the man in a rescue harness before both are hoisted to safety.
The man was taken to the riverbank, where fire personnel were waiting, according to the sheriff's office.
The helicopter's pilot, Rich Dickner, told CBS News that the water was quickly rising around the vehicle.
"We didn't waste much time," Dickner said.
"As opposed to when we first got there, you can see the water line on the video — it's below the window — and it had risen up to the top of the window," he continued. "So there was that urgency."
People Magazine reported that Deputy Lindsey Smith was lowered approximately 80 feet from the helicopter toward the overturned truck.
She initially struggled to get her footing before securing herself to the vehicle, according to the report.
The entire rescue took less than five minutes, authorities said.
The Maricopa County Sheriff's Office credited the crew's swift response with getting the man to safety.
"Thanks to the skill and quick response of our Aviation crew, the subject was safely brought to shore," the sheriff's office said.
The Weather Channel reported that remnants of Hurricane Polo brought historic rainfall to parts of the Desert Southwest, contributing to dangerous flash flooding.
The Flood Control District of Maricopa County warned drivers not to attempt to cross flooded roads.
"Remember: Conditions can change fast. If you encounter a flooded roadway, Turn Around, Don't Drown."
Fox News Digital has reached out to the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office for additional information.

articles.title: Australian couple among passengers on diverted flydubai flight to Israel, embassy says
articles.author: Tess Ikonomou

paras.en: Two Australian citizens were onboard a flight to Tel Aviv that was diverted after one of the pilots allegedly stabbed the other in an attack, according to the Israeli embassy.
The passengers are a Jewish couple from Sydney, the embassy in Australia confirmed to the Guardian on Thursday. No further details were provided.
The flydubai aircraft was travelling from the United Arab Emirates to Israel when it was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
One of the pilots, whom Israeli officials said was an Omani citizen, is accused of stabbing his co-pilot. During the alleged attack, the plane plunged about 17,000 feet in just two minutes.

Passenger Yaniv Hayoun later recounted how he and other passengers heard screaming and felt pressure as the plane dived before forcing their way into the cockpit and finding the attacker at the instrument panel.

“I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and dragged him out first,” Hayoun said during a meeting with Netanyahu after the plane had landed safely and the passengers were flown to Israel. “He was trying to destroy the instruments to disable the plane.”
Israel’s ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, said the incident reminded him of the 11 September attacks.
“You have here a very special incident, and due to the real heroism of some people on board, they were saved.”
Newman said heightened security alerts had been issued following the attack.
“It just shows that … those that hate Israel also hate the peace.
“It’s an attempt to hit at the peace itself, at the Abraham Accords, and the relationships which Israel does have with Arab and Muslim countries.”
The Abraham Accords normalised relations between the UAE and Israel in 2020.
Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said it was too early to tell who was ultimately behind the the incident.
There are about 12,000 Australian citizens living in Israel and 25,000 in the UAE.

articles.title: Australia news live: Anika Wells named in Time’s ‘influential rising stars’; NSW seeks to join Queensland in ‘from the river to the sea’ ban case
articles.author: Achol Arok (now) and Nick Visser (earlier)

paras.en: Anika Wells named as part of Time 100 ‘most influential rising stars’ list
paras.zh: Anika Wells入选时代100 “最具影响力新星”榜单

paras.en: The federal communications minister, Anika Wells, has been named as one of Time magazine’s “world’s most influential rising stars”, as part of its annual Time 100 list.

Wells, who has overseen the under-16s social media ban and is now working on a world-leading digital duty of care framework, was included on what Time calls its list of “leaders who are shaping the future”.
Also on the list: musicians Sombr and PinkPantheress, soccer player Folarin Balogun, US senator Andy Kim, the Dutch prime minister, Rob Jetten, and Donald Trump’s political adviser James Blair.
Wells was published in the list alongside a testimonial written by the former Labor PM Julia Gillard:

As the world grapples with the extraordinary power of social media and the increasingly pervasive role it plays, Anika Wells has emerged as one of the most significant voices in a growing global movement to reframe the relationship between technology and the well-being of our children.

Even in the face of intense opposition from some of the world’s largest tech companies, she remains steadfast … Future generations will look back on her landmark changes as courageous and trail-blazing.
Australian musician Troye Sivan was also included on the “influential rising stars” list, with a testimonial written by Kylie Minogue. She wrote:
Troye Sivan is a perfect 2020s pop star… Troye doesn’t just make pop music to love. He makes pop music to believe in.
Jetstar staff to escalate industrial action with one-hour stoppages

Jetstar staff will escalate industrial action tomorrow, with union members planning one-hour stoppages at major airports nationwide and abstaining from routine duties. It coincides with school holidays and the start of the NRL grand final weekend.

Australian Services Union (ASU) confirmed members will cease passenger announcements and flight disruption management, while processing eligible fees for excess baggage, seat selection and late changes at $0.

The union said the escalation follows failed negotiations over pay and conditions. Members took industrial action in September, after voting in favour of seeking wages in-line with other Qantas Group staff, higher penalty rates, improved leave, job security and better weather protections.

ASU assistant national secretary, Scott Cowen said members were “left with no other choice”, amid cost-of-living pressures and extreme weather conditions. He said the airline failed to support workers with extra weather protections or a pay offer that responds to this crisis properly”.

Jetstar’s domestic earnings are up 15 per cent this year on record passenger numbers, and Qantas Group is turning a profit. A 2.1% pay rise for the people who made that possible is not what a fair share looks like.
Jetstar has the money and the record year to make this right.”
Jetstar said it does not expect any impact on flights, citing “strong contingency plans.

A spokesperson for the airline said it was “very disappointing” the union chose to pursue further action despite a “comprehensive and fair offer, including meaningful pay increases, improved penalties and allowances, and greater rostering flexibility”.
South Australia’s AI royal commission board selected
A former judge and two global tech experts will lead a royal commission into artificial intelligence after the most “substantial technological shift” in two centuries, AAP reports.
The South Australian government on Thursday revealed the terms of reference for the state inquiry and its pick for chair, the economist and former judge IainRoss.
Kate Pounder and Christopher Manning were selected as commissioners for their expertise in technology policy, innovation, computer science and machine learning.
Ross said the inquiry would balance opportunities for enriching lives, improving productivity and lifting economic performance with an approach that mitigated risks and threats.
Manning, a world-renowned AI expert, is the co-founder of the Stanford Institute for Human-Centred AI and a professor in machine learning at the private research university.
Premier Peter Malinauskas said it was impossible to put the “AI genie back in the bottle”, conceding the fast-developing technology sometimes scared him.
If we don’t contemplate … an AI future forcefully, there could be really severe consequences, as well as a big opportunity cost.
Pill testing at NSW music festivals to return this weekend
The New South Wales government’s reinstated pill testing service at selected music festivals will return to this long weekend’s Knockout Outdoor festival.
The $4.3m initiative will operate at up to 15 festivals each year, selected by NSW Health in consultation with the music fesitval industry and harm-reduction organisations.

The government reiterated that “illicit drugs remain illegal in NSW” and said the service “is not an endorsement of illicit drug use”. It also reminded festivalgoers that there “will always be risks involved when consuming these substances”.
The state’s chief health officer, Dr Kerry Chant, said drug checking services could help people make more informed decisions, but did not guarantee safety. She said:
Drug checking services are intended to help people make informed decisions to reduce drug-related harm, but they are not a guarantee of safety.

Our priority is to reduce harm and keep people safe. Drug checking at music festivals aims to educate individuals, allowing them to avoid dangerous substances and make safer and more informed choices.
RBA denies staff real wages increase after interest rate rise
The Reserve Bank rejected its own staff’s requests for a real pay rise and back pay on lost wages just hours after it hiked interest rates on Tuesday.

While the RBA has repeatedly warned that inflation-matched wage growth risks pushing up consumer prices, its employees argue the bank’s own forecasts show their pay will slip behind the cost of living.
As staff left the office on Tuesday evening, the governor, Michele Bullock, emailed them asking them to vote for a pay offer nearly identical to one already rejected by 54% of staff in July.
Anti-racism training in schools among youth justice reforms needed in Victoria, working group says

A group of South Sudanese Australian leaders in Victoria have called for mandatory anti-racism training for all school staff and ramped up efforts to target organised crime groups preying on young people to reduce the over-representation of the community’s children in the justice system.

The recommendations are contained within a report by the state’s South Sudanese Australian Youth Justice Expert Working Group report, delivered to the state government earlier this year and released publicly on Thursday.
The report contains 59 recommendations designed to reduce the over-representation of South Sudanese Australians in the state’s youth justice system.
The government has established a committee to oversee the implementation of the recommendations. But its response has not outlined which specific recommendations it has accepted.

The state government said it had already commenced work on some of the recommendations while some required “policy, funding, cultural and operational implications that require careful consideration and planning”.

Victoria’s youth justice minister, Ros Spence, said the government was working with the South Sudanese community to stop crime before it starts and ensure “young people have the support to stay on the right path”:
Our response is the result of listening to South Sudanese young people, families, and community leaders. We thank them for their leadership and for putting forward practical solutions.
NSW seeks to join Queensland in defence of ban on ‘from the river to the sea’

The NSW government has sought leave to join the Queensland government in a high court case brought by pro-Palestine protesters against laws banning the contested phrases “from the river to the sea” and “globalise the intifada”.

A spokesperson for the NSW attorney-general, Michael Daley, confirmed that the government had sought to be a party to the case alongside the Queensland government, but declined to comment further. High court listings show the attorney general filed leave to intervene in the case last week.
In a statement, Remah Naji, a spokesperson for Justice for Palestine Magan-djin, who brought the challenge, said:

What the NSW government fails to understand is that by intervening, they’re playing directly into our hands. This intervention was expected. We will use it to transform this from a Queensland case into a national struggle, one in which all people of conscience have a stake.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics released new figures this morning showing job vacancies fell again in August 2026.
Vacancies sat at 325,000, according to quarterly figures, Sean Crick, the ABS head of labour statistics, said:
The decline in job vacancies was driven by the private sector, notably in business goods and services. This was offset somewhat by rises in customer facing roles including in Retail trade.
Over the year, job vacancies declined by 1.3%. The wholesale trade industry had the largest quarterly drop, of 18%, followed by professional, scientific and technical services, down 17.3%.
The largest percentage rises in job vacancies were in retail trade, up 24.5%, followed by financial and insurance services, up by 14.1%.
Israel issues ‘heightened alerts’ after flydubai attack
Israel’s ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, says his nation will tighten security following the alleged stabbing attack on a flight en route to Tel Aviv.
The top diplomat said it will be alleged the Omani co-pilot involved in the attack had attempted to crash the plane.
This is a heightened alert period, and of course … Israel will take the precautions.
Prime minister Netanyahu gave a briefing last night, in which he said that there is heightened security alerts.

The Reserve Bank has warned that a sudden loss of faith in the artificial intelligence boom could trigger “disorderly asset price corrections” and that “Australia is unlikely to be immune” from the impact.
The RBA’s latest financial stability review said “threats to global financial stability continue to mount”.

Alongside the huge sums being invested in AI, two ongoing conflicts – in the Middle East and Ukraine – alongside “intensifying strategic competition among major powers” underscored these threats, the RBA said.
High valuations in global corporate debt and share markets meant they were vulnerable to a “disorderly” correction.

“One possible trigger could be a shift in sentiment towards the AI investment boom, which is increasingly fuelled by expectations of sustained rapid earnings growth and a debt-financing cycle that is becoming more opaque and circular,” the report said.
The RBA also warned of the rising risk of cyber-attacks, potentially facilitated by AI, and a sudden sell-off in global bond markets.
These external factors are the most prominent threats to financial stability in Australia.
Sydney’s metro extension meets key safety approvals – but some doors won’t open

The NSW transport minister, John Graham, says the highly anticipated southwest extension of the Sydney Metro has received key safety approvals, but after discussions with the safety regulator, six doors on the line will not be in use when it opens later this year.
Providing an update at a press conference this morning, Graham said:

As part of the initial safety case when first passengers jump on this train, we’ve agreed with [the Office of the National Rail Safety Regulator] that six of those doors will stay closed, so that there’s no even minor safety issues as this runs …
They’ll be clearly signed so passengers know just one of the safety measures in place for this complex build that we’re undertaking on what is a 130-year-old railway.
They include three sets of doors at Dulwich Hill, and one each at Marrickville, Canterbury and Campsie. Graham said it was an “ongoing discussion” whether these doors will eventually be in use.

The issue relates to mechanical “gap-fillers” that have been added to fill the space between the train and curved platforms on the historic line, with the issue affecting doors where those gaps are widest. There are 360 doors across the 10 stations that are part of the extension, with 18 on each platform at Dulwich Hill.
This morning, Graham said “we’re confident we’ll be able to operate this railway safely very shortly”.
No sign of negative equity crisis despite property slump
The Reserve Bank estimates that fewer than one in 100 borrowers owe more on their home than its worth, despite this year’s broadening price falls.
The RBA in its latest financial stability review said Australia’s household sector was largely coping well with rising interest rates and a recent decline in real incomes. The biannual report said:

While some households continue to experience hardship, the estimated share of mortgagors in severe financial stress or in arrears has, so far, remained low, supported by the strong labour market and mortgagors’ savings and equity buffers.

The RBA’s estimate that fewer than 1% of borrowers were in “negative equity” came with the caveat: recent buyers who took out loans worth close to the value of the property were more likely to now be in the position where the mortgage was higher than their home’s market value.

This included those who took advantage of the government’s 5% home guarantee scheme, the RBA said, although evidence suggested that the share of these borrowers falling behind on their payments remained “contained”.

The RBA estimated that even a 20% property price crash would only push about 5% of mortgages into negative equity – a testament to the fact most homeowners have enjoyed significant value gains over the years. The report said:
Negative equity is insufficient to trigger default if borrowers remain able to service their loans, which remains the case for the vast majority of these households.

Wells, who has overseen the under-16s social media ban and is now working on a world-leading digital duty of care framework, was included on what Time calls its list of “leaders who are shaping the future”.
Also on the list: musicians Sombr and PinkPantheress, soccer player Folarin Balogun, US senator Andy Kim, the Dutch prime minister, Rob Jetten, and Donald Trump’s political adviser James Blair.
